criterion_notes.c1: Examines rural household sanitation facility coverage (unimproved, improved, and sewer/septic-connected toilets) across 154 countries, forecasting coverage trends to 2030 via univariate ARIMA time-series models and using unsafe sanitation prevalence as an exposure in disease-burden modeling.
criterion_notes.c2: Fails BOTH the plain wording of Criterion 2 and the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading. Under the plain wording, although 'Lacking Sanitation Governance' appears in the title and abstract, the empirical analysis does not measure, model, or evaluate any legal, administrative, institutional, regulatory, or governance factor; the modeled inputs are strictly demographic variables (population size, age structure), Sociodemographic Index, historical sanitation coverage, and diarrheal mortality rates, while governance laws and agencies (e.g., US Clean Water Act, China's Toilet Revolution) are mentioned only briefly as policy recommendations in Section 3.4. Under the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading, no rule-type mechanism governing service access (such as eligibility screening, tenure/documentation rules, tariffs, administrative burden, enforcement, or regulatory structure) is examined—at most unanalysed macro-governance background rhetoric is present.
criterion_notes.c3: Quantitative empirical secondary-data modeling study integrating WHO rural sanitation monitoring data and Global Burden of Disease (GBD) 2021 epidemiological data across 154 countries using Comparable Risk Assessment, Bayesian age-period-cohort (BAPC) models, ARIMA forecasting, and decomposition analysis.
criterion_notes.c4: The study's modeled dependent outcome is epidemiological mortality—Deaths Attributable to Unsafe Sanitation in Rural areas (DAUSRs) and age-standardized diarrheal death rates—where rural sanitation coverage serves as an environmental risk exposure/driver rather than a service-access outcome explained by any governance factor (only univariate ARIMA extrapolations of historical sanitation series are reported as intermediate inputs).
criterion_notes.c5: Population and unit of analysis (national rural populations stratified by age group across 154 countries, 2000-2030), study exposures/drivers (unsafe rural sanitation prevalence, population size, age structure, baseline diarrheal mortality rates), study outcome (DAUSRs and age-standardized diarrheal mortality rates), and study design (ecological burden-of-disease modeling and decomposition analysis) are clearly identifiable.

evidence_quotes.quote: Exposure to unsafe sanitation was defined based on the type of toilet used in rural households. Sanitation facilities were categorized into three distinct types: unimproved, improved, and those connected to sewerage or septic systems
Despite improvements in global rural sanitation, it is projected that by 2030, 12.2% of the rural population will still lack access to sanitary toilets and will persist in open defecation practices

we employed a decomposition technique to quantify the effects of age structure, population size, prevalence of rural sanitation facilities, and associated disease mortality rates on disease-related fatalities.

For example, the United States implemented the Clean Water Act (USEPA), while China has initiated its “Toilet Revolution”, and Finland, South Korea, Japan, Singapore, and the United States have established dedicated agencies for the management of public restrooms.
We retrieved mortality rates from diarrhea, relative risks (RR), and Sociodemographic Index (SDI) data from 2000 to 2020 for 204 countries globally from the GBD 2021 database.

raw_response.exposure: Unsafe rural household sanitation facility prevalence (unimproved, improved, sewer/septic connection), population size, rural age structure (aging >65 and children <5), and diarrheal disease mortality rates (no legal or governance exposure studied)
raw_response.outcome: Deaths Attributable to Unsafe Sanitation in Rural areas (DAUSRs) and age-standardized diarrheal mortality rates (with intermediate univariate ARIMA time-series projections of rural sanitation facility proportions)
raw_response.population_and_sample: National rural populations stratified by age group across 154 countries globally (country-year ecological panel and projections, 2000-2030)
raw_response.rationale: Excluded under E03 (Wrong exposure; also models a mortality outcome rather than determinants of service access). Despite referencing 'Lacking Sanitation Governance' in the title, this global burden-of-disease study empirically models only demographic dynamics (population size, aging, fertility), historical rural sanitation prevalence, and diarrheal mortality rates to estimate and decompose Deaths Attributable to Unsafe Sanitation in Rural areas (DAUSRs) across 154 countries from 2000 to 2030. No legal, administrative, institutional, regulatory, or governance factor is measured or analyzed under either the plain wording or the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading of Criterion 2, and rural sanitation coverage functions as an epidemiological exposure for diarrheal mortality rather than an access outcome governed by legal/administrative rules.
raw_response.study_design: Ecological global burden-of-disease modeling, time-series forecasting (BAPC and ARIMA), and decomposition analysis using secondary WHO and GBD 2021 data
